title: Stage 3: per-tenant limits and retries
summary: One noisy tenant may not run more than its share at once, and transient failures are retried with backoff while permanent ones fail fast.

steps.title: The brief
body: The pipeline is shared by many customers (tenants). Last week one tenant's import queued 50,000 jobs and their slow API calls
occupied every worker. And a partner that times out now and then turns into a wall of `Failed`.
Add to `PipelineOptions`, as `init` properties with defaults that keep stages 1 and 2 working:
public int MaxPerTenant { get; init; } = int.MaxValue;              // jobs of one tenant running at once
public int MaxAttempts { get; init; } = 1;                           // 1 = no retries
public Func<int, TimeSpan> Backoff { get; init; } = _ => TimeSpan.Zero; // wait before retry n (n = 1, 2, ...)
public Func<TimeSpan, CancellationToken, Task> Delay { get; init; } = Task.Delay;
- At most `MaxPerTenant` jobs of the **same** `Job.Tenant` run at once (a `SemaphoreSlim` per tenant, in a `ConcurrentDictionary`).
- A handler that throws **`TimeoutException`** is retried, up to `MaxAttempts` calls, waiting `await Delay(Backoff(n), token)`
before retry *n*; any other exception fails the job at once. A job that succeeds on a retry counts once, as `Processed`.

steps.prompt: A worker waits on tenant A's semaphore while A is at its limit. What is the cost of this simple design?
options: That worker sits idle even if tenant B has jobs queued behind it (head-of-line blocking)
Tenant A can exceed its limit
steps.explain: The limit holds, but a worker waits instead of doing B's work. Production systems use a queue per tenant and pick fairly between them (round robin, weighted). For this stage the simple version is fine; say the trade-off out loud in review.

steps.prompt: Match each policy to the failure it protects against.
pairs: one customer's burst taking every worker
memory growing without limit during an outage
a partner that times out now and then
a deploy that waits forever for a stuck job

steps.title: Fair and resilient
prompt: Add `MaxPerTenant`, `MaxAttempts`, `Backoff` and `Delay` to `PipelineOptions` as in the brief, and make `Pipeline` honour them:
- a `SemaphoreSlim(MaxPerTenant)` per tenant, taken before the handler and released in `finally` (wait for it with the
- retries of `TimeoutException` only, up to `MaxAttempts` calls, waiting `Delay(Backoff(n), token)` before retry *n*.

solution: record Job(string Id, string Tenant, string Payload);
record PipelineOptions(int Capacity, int Workers, TimeSpan EnqueueWait)
public int MaxPerTenant { get; init; } = int.MaxValue;
public Func<int, TimeSpan> Backoff { get; init; } = _ => TimeSpan.Zero;
public Func<TimeSpan, CancellationToken, Task> Delay { get; init; } = Task.Delay;
class Pipeline(PipelineOptions options, Func<Job, CancellationToken, Task> handle)
private readonly CancellationTokenSource _abort = new();   // the drain deadline
public async ValueTask<bool> TryEnqueueAsync(Job job, CancellationToken ct)
Interlocked.Increment(ref _failed);   // permanent failure, retries used up, or cut off by the drain deadline
template: static async Task Until(Func<bool> ok) { for (var i = 0; i < 200 && !ok(); i++) await Task.Delay(10); }
await Dojo.TryAsync("Stages 1 and 2 still work", async () =>
var p = new Pipeline(new PipelineOptions(4, 3, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)), async (job, ct) =>
for (var i = 0; i < 12; i++) await p.TryEnqueueAsync(new Job($"j{i}", $"t{i % 3}", i == 5 ? "boom" : "ok"), CancellationToken.None);
Dojo.Check("No jobs accepted after StopAsync", !await p.TryEnqueueAsync(new Job("late", "t1", "ok"), CancellationToken.None), "");
await Dojo.TryAsync("One tenant at a time per tenant, tenants in parallel", async () =>
var p = new Pipeline(new PipelineOptions(10, 4, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)) { MaxPerTenant = 1 }, async (job, ct) =>
foreach (var id in new[] { "a1", "a2", "a3", "b1", "b2", "b3" }) await p.TryEnqueueAsync(new Job(id, id[..1], "x"), CancellationToken.None);
Dojo.Eq("Tenants a and b each run one job at once", 2, Volatile.Read(ref inFlight));
Dojo.Eq("No tenant ever ran two at once", "a:1 b:1", $"a:{peaks.GetValueOrDefault("a")} b:{peaks.GetValueOrDefault("b")}");
await Dojo.TryAsync("Transient failures are retried with backoff", async () =>
var p = new Pipeline(options, async (job, ct) =>
if (job.Id == "flaky" && n < 3) throw new TimeoutException("partner slow");
foreach (var id in new[] { "flaky", "bad", "dead" }) await p.TryEnqueueAsync(new Job(id, "t1", "x"), CancellationToken.None);
Dojo.Eq("flaky succeeds on its 3rd attempt", 3, attempts.GetValueOrDefault("flaky"));
Dojo.Eq("dead gives up after MaxAttempts", 3, attempts.GetValueOrDefault("dead"));
Dojo.Eq("Waits follow the backoff (flaky, then dead)", "100,200,100,200", string.Join(",", waits.Select(w => (int)w.TotalMilliseconds)));
await Dojo.TryAsync("The drain deadline still cuts off a stuck job", async () =>
var p = new Pipeline(new PipelineOptions(4, 1, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)) { MaxPerTenant = 1 }, async (job, ct) => { started.TrySetResult(); await Task.Delay(Timeout.Infinite, ct); });
Dojo.Check("StopAsync returns", await Task.WhenAny(stop, Task.Delay(3000)) == stop, "Still waiting 3 seconds after the deadline.");
Dojo.Eq("The cut-off job counts as failed", 1, p.Failed);
hints: Turn `PipelineOptions` into a record with a body and four `init` properties with the defaults from the brief.

In `RunOneAsync`: `var gate = _tenants.GetOrAdd(job.Tenant, _ => new SemaphoreSlim(options.MaxPerTenant));`, `await gate.WaitAsync(_abort.Token)`, then the handler in a `try` with `finally { gate.Release(); }`.

Retry loop: `for (var attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { await handle(...); ...; return; } catch (TimeoutException) when (attempt < options.MaxAttempts) { await options.Delay(options.Backoff(attempt), _abort.Token); } }`.
explain: You now have the core of what libraries like Hangfire, MassTransit's in-memory transport or a `BackgroundService` + `Channel` setup
give you: bounded intake, a worker pool, graceful drain, fairness and retries, each with a test that forces the interleaving it is
about. In an interview, this is the system to sketch when asked "how would you process jobs in the background?", trade-offs included
(in-memory jobs are lost on a crash: use a durable queue or an outbox when that matters).
